lesson.title: The Activated Complex: Chemistry's Most Unstable Moment
lesson.summary: Describes the fleeting, high-energy arrangement of atoms sitting at the peak of the energy barrier, where old bonds are breaking and new bonds are forming at the same time.
lesson.body:
The activated complex is the unstable, high energy arrangement of atoms that exists momentarily at the very peak of the reaction energy diagram, right at the top of the activation energy barrier described in the previous section. In this arrangement, bonds within the original reactants are in the process of breaking while new bonds toward the products are in the process of forming, simultaneously. That makes the activated complex neither reactant nor product; it is a strange in-between structure that cannot be isolated, bottled, or observed sitting still the way an ordinary stable compound can.

Part of why it cannot be isolated is sheer speed. The activated complex persists for an extraordinarily brief instant, on the order of 10^-13 to 10^-14 seconds, roughly the timescale of a single molecular bond vibration, far too fast to capture with ordinary laboratory techniques (specialized ultrafast laser spectroscopy has been used by researchers to study transition state like species on timescales this short, though that lies well beyond the scope of this course). This briefness is exactly why it is called "activated": it exists only for the instant it takes to convert the reactant bonds into product bonds, and then it is gone, either falling back down to reactants again or continuing on to products.

Worked example, continuing directly from the energy diagram numbers introduced with activation energy: peak energy = 125 kJ/mol, Ea (forward) = 85 kJ/mol, Ea (reverse) = 115 kJ/mol, both already computed in the previous section. These two barrier heights are connected to the overall reaction energy change by simple subtraction:

Ea (forward) - Ea (reverse) = 85 - 115 = -30 kJ/mol

Compare that to the overall reaction energy change computed in the previous section: products minus reactants = 10 - 40 = -30 kJ/mol. The two numbers match exactly. This is not a coincidence, and it will always hold true: the height of the activated complex above the reactants, minus its height above the products, equals the net energy change of the reaction as a whole. It is also a genuinely useful check on your own work: if a forward and reverse activation energy do not reproduce the correct overall reaction energy change this way, an arithmetic or diagram-reading mistake has been made somewhere along the line.

The energy and structure of the activated complex is exactly what a catalyst manipulates to speed up a reaction, by opening up an alternative pathway with a lower energy activated complex sitting at the top, without permanently changing the identity of the reactants or products themselves. That idea belongs to a different part of the kinetics unit, but it is worth flagging here because it underscores just how central the activated complex is to everything about how fast, or how slowly, a reaction proceeds.
